Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

**Plan A:** Volunteers meet at the north access point, work west to east, and leave filled bags by the parking lot for pickup.

**Plan B:** The shoreline is split into three zones. Teams start at the central access point and carry filled bags to the north lot.

**Plan C:** Volunteers start at the south end and work toward the fenced nesting area, stopping at the fence. Bags are picked up from the south lot.

- Volunteer walking distance
- Access for the collection vehicle
- Risk of disturbing the fenced nesting area
- Ease of coordinating teams

Do not perform the task.", "input": "please make a concise but useful summary of the supplied packet about the archaeology museum's North Quay excavation and the objects now in its study collection. the packet is a mix of a site note, field sheets, object cards, conservation notes, two interview transcripts and a council letter, so don't make it sound like one person wrote it all. around 600 to 800 words would be good. this is for people who know the museum but haven't followed this project, and it should be understandable without specialist archaeology language. the packet says the excavation took place on the east edge of the museum's old harbor grounds, beside the brick storehouse and about 40 metres north of the current gallery entrance. the museum began the work in april 2019 before a drainage trench was replaced. the trench was 18 metres long and 1.2 metres wide. the field sheets date the main excavation to 8 april through 3 may, but one photograph has a handwritten date of 6 may and no explanation. say that these dates don't quite match rather than making them agree. the site note says the ground had been used for storage and repair work since at least the late 1800s, and that modern paving covered most of the area until it was removed. a plan marks a timber platform on the north side and a stone drain running west to east. don't say the platform and drain are definitely from the same period, the packet doesn't establish that.

there are three recorded layers in the field sheets. layer one is compact gravel and broken brick, 10 to 24 centimetres deep, with modern nails, a bottle top marked 1987 and fragments of blue-and-white tile. layer two is dark sandy soil with charcoal flecks, fish bone and pieces of coarse pottery; it runs beneath the storehouse wall in two squares, but the sheets say the wall was not disturbed. layer three is pale silt with small rounded stones, seen only at the southern end of the trench. on 17 april the crew found a shallow posthole in layer two, 22 centimetres across and 19 centimetres deep. its fill contained a small iron hook and two hazelnut shells. there is no lab date for either shell, and the field lead wrote “could be a fixing point, but we can't tell from this cut alone.” retain that uncertainty. three days later rain entered the trench and work was paused for a day; the log says a pump was used, not that the trench flooded.

object cards list 46 catalogued finds from the trench, though the packet also says that a number of unmarked pottery fragments were returned to the soil sample bags and not counted. the largest group is 21 pottery sherds, mostly plain grey ware, with four pieces of a rim that may come from one vessel. a card describes a stamped red-clay fragment as “possibly a maker's mark”; the stamp is incomplete and no maker is named. other listed finds are 12 iron fasteners, 5 glass fragments, 3 fish bones, 2 worked flint flakes, the hook and one lead weight. the weight is 31 grams and has a small hole through its narrow end. don't call it a fishing weight as a fact; one handwritten card says it might have been used on a line, while a later note says its use is unknown. the packet doesn't give a final interpretation for the pottery or the flint.

conservation notes say the iron hook and fasteners were dry-brushed, photographed and placed in separate labelled boxes on 22 may 2019. the hook has active orange corrosion and was not treated with chemicals. the lead weight was rinsed with distilled water and air-dried. one glass fragment has a chipped edge, and the notes say it was packed in tissue before being moved to the study room. there are no conservation records for the pottery sherds or the bones. don't imply that every object was conserved in the same way, or that the collection is on public display; the object cards call it a study collection.

one interview is with former storehouse worker Elsie Ward, recorded 11 june 2019. she remembers “a little wooden landing where we stacked the nets” near the north wall, but says she left the job in 1978 and cannot remember when it was built. the second interview is with retired harbor engineer Tomas Bell, recorded 19 june. he recalls a drain being cleared in the 1960s, but isn't sure whether it was this drain or one closer to the road. include those as recollections, not confirmation of the excavation dates or features. a council letter dated 2 april 2019 gives permission to open the trench subject to keeping the storehouse wall untouched and returning the paved walkway to use by 10 may. a museum email dated 9 may says the walkway was reopened that afternoon. don't say the council inspected it or approved the work afterward; there is no such record in this packet.

there's also this numbered section in the packet, keep its points recognizable in the summary: 1. the trench was opened for drainage work, not as a planned search for a particular object. 2. the posthole, pottery and drain are recorded, but their dates and relationships aren't settled. 3. the museum has kept the finds for study and says nothing here about a public exhibition. please keep the summary focused on what the packet records, distinguish written observations from the two people's memories, and mention gaps where they're relevant. ordinary terms are better than adding technical interpretation. don't add an opening claim about what the site proves, and don't turn the possible explanations on the cards into firm conclusions.", "output": "Please write a clear, concise summary of the supplied packet about the archaeology museum’s North Quay excavation and the objects in its study collection. Aim for 600–800 words. The intended readers know the museum but have not followed this project, so use understandable language and avoid specialist archaeology terms where ordinary ones will do. The packet combines a site note, field sheets, object cards, conservation notes, two interview transcripts, and a council letter; do not present them as though they were all written by one person.

Cover the recorded excavation setting and timeline. The work began in April 2019 before replacement of a drainage trench on the east edge of the museum’s old harbor grounds, beside the brick storehouse and about 40 metres north of the current gallery entrance. The trench was 18 metres long and 1.2 metres wide. Field sheets date the main excavation from 8 April to 3 May, while a photograph is handwritten “6 May” with no explanation. Note that the dates do not quite match. The site note says the ground had been used for storage and repair since at least the late 1800s, and modern paving covered most of it until removal. A plan marks a timber platform on the north side and a west-to-east stone drain; the packet does not establish that they are from the same period.

Summarize the three recorded layers and the main field observations. Layer one is 10–24 centimetres of compact gravel and broken brick, with modern nails, a bottle top marked 1987, and blue-and-white tile fragments. Layer two is dark sandy soil with charcoal flecks, fish bone, and coarse pottery pieces; it extends beneath the storehouse wall in two squares, but the wall was not disturbed. Layer three is pale silt with small rounded stones, recorded only at the trench’s southern end. On 17 April, the crew found a 22-centimetre-wide, 19-centimetre-deep shallow posthole in layer two. Its fill held a small iron hook and two hazelnut shells. Neither shell has a lab date. Retain the field lead’s uncertainty: “could be a fixing point, but we can't tell from this cut alone.” The 20 April log says rain entered the trench, work paused for a day, and a pump was used; it does not say the trench flooded.

Describe the finds without assigning them unsupported meanings. The object cards list 46 catalogued finds, while noting that unmarked pottery fragments returned to soil sample bags were not counted. There are 21 pottery sherds, mostly plain grey ware, including four rim pieces that may be from one vessel. A stamped red-clay fragment is described as “possibly a maker's mark”; the stamp is incomplete and no maker is named. The remaining listed finds are 12 iron fasteners, 5 glass fragments, 3 fish bones, 2 worked flint flakes, the hook, and a 31-gram lead weight with a small hole through its narrow end. One handwritten card suggests the weight might have been used on a line; a later note says its use is unknown. Do not state that it was a fishing weight. The packet gives no final interpretation of the pottery or flint.

Include the conservation records: on 22 May 2019 the iron hook and fasteners were dry-brushed, photographed, and put in separate labelled boxes. The hook has active orange corrosion and received no chemical treatment. The lead weight was rinsed with distilled water and air-dried. One chipped-edge glass fragment was wrapped in tissue before transfer to the study room. There are no conservation records for the pottery or bones. Do not imply that all objects received the same treatment or that they are on public display; the cards describe a study collection.

Distinguish interview memories from written observations. Former storehouse worker Elsie Ward, interviewed on 11 June 2019, recalls “a little wooden landing where we stacked the nets” near the north wall. She left the job in 1978 and cannot recall when it was built. Retired harbor engineer Tomas Bell, interviewed on 19 June, remembers a drain being cleared in the 1960s but is unsure whether it was this drain or one nearer the road. These recollections do not confirm the excavation dates or features.

Mention the administrative records accurately. A council letter dated 2 April 2019 permitted the trench subject to leaving the storehouse wall untouched and reopening the paved walkway by 10 May. A museum email dated 9 May says the walkway reopened that afternoon. The packet contains no record of a later council inspection or approval.

Keep the three points in the packet’s numbered section recognizable: (1) the trench was opened for drainage work, not to search for a particular object; (2) the posthole, pottery, and drain are recorded, but their dates and relationships are unsettled; and (3) the museum retained the finds for study, with no statement here about a public exhibition. The questions should encourage people to share different views, not make a speech or lead the group toward a decision. Cover how people find and choose books to share, what could make the exchange welcoming to neighbors with different reading interests, and what practical factors might make it easier to participate. Do not assume the exchange already has particular rules, a fixed location, or an established way of operating; include questions that help the group discuss what might work. Keep the questions focused on the neighborhood book exchange, rather than book clubs or reading in general. Do not perform the task.", "input": "Write a practical field guide for the volunteer crew responsible for sorting, weighing, and recording debris during a fictional coastal cleanup at Gull Point. The guide is for a single Saturday event and should help people carry out the task consistently, including volunteers who have not done a cleanup before. Do not write a general essay about marine pollution or add activities outside debris handling and recording. Use plain, respectful language that can be read quickly at a staging table or checked on a phone in the field.

The cleanup runs from 8:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The sorting station is on the gravel apron beside the south parking lot, about 60 metres inland from the beach access gate. The site has four folding tables, two platform scales, washable tubs, heavy-duty bags, nitrile gloves in assorted sizes, litter grabbers, clipboards, pencils, chalk, and a handwashing jug with soap. There is no electricity or running water at the station. The event lead is Mara Chen; the debris-recording lead is Luis Ortega. Volunteers should ask either lead if a container, item, or record is unclear rather than guessing.

The beach team will bring debris to the station in tied bags or reusable tubs. Bags and tubs should stay in the marked staging area until a sorting pair is ready to process them. Do not open an unknown or suspicious container, handle medical waste, or pick up sharp objects by hand. Set such items aside without disturbing them and notify Mara. The guide should distinguish this stop-and-notify procedure from ordinary sorting, without suggesting that volunteers investigate or dispose of hazardous material themselves. It should also explain that volunteers should not put hands into opaque bags or tubs before checking for sharp or unsafe contents with a grabber.

Please organize the guide as a usable sequence from station setup through the last record check. Include a short opening summary of the task, a materials checklist based only on the supplies listed here, and clear roles for the event lead, recording lead, and sorting pairs. There are 18 volunteers in total: two leads and 16 volunteers. The crew can form four sorting pairs, with the other eight volunteers rotating between bringing in containers, weighing, recording, and taking brief breaks. Explain a simple rotation that fits this crew and avoids leaving the recording sheet unattended. Do not assign medical, transport, or disposal duties that have not been specified.

For ordinary debris, ask sorting pairs to separate items into these categories: plastic, metal, glass, paper and cardboard, fishing gear, and mixed or unclassifiable. Keep fishing gear separate even when it contains plastic or metal. If an item clearly belongs to another listed category, use that category; if its material or category is genuinely unclear, use mixed or unclassifiable and add a short note. Do not require volunteers to identify resin codes, brands, or exact product types. Keep each category in a separate tub or bag, and use chalk labels that remain readable if a paper label gets damp. Explain how to keep glass contained and how to avoid compressing bags before they are weighed. Do not invent a recycling destination or claim that any category will be recycled.

The guide must give a repeatable weighing and tally procedure. Each filled category container is weighed on a platform scale, with the empty container’s weight subtracted if it is included in the reading. The scales display kilograms to one decimal place. Record net weight in kilograms, category, container or batch number, and the time weighed. Count individual items only for the following three groups: beverage bottles, food wrappers, and fishing line or net fragments. For each group, record a whole-number count; do not estimate counts for other categories. A person recording should read the category and weight aloud to a second person, who checks the display and the written entry before the container is moved. If the scale reading shifts or a number is uncertain, pause and weigh again rather than entering an approximate value.

Use a numbered section titled “Record and handoff” to specify what the clipboard sheet should contain and how to check it before the station closes. The sheet should include the date, site name, recorder’s initials, batch number, category, net weight, any required item count, time weighed, and a brief note for mixed or unclassifiable material or an interrupted weighing. Leave unknown information blank and flag it for Luis; do not fill gaps by inference. Have the recording lead check that batch numbers are not duplicated, category and units are present, and any recorded count belongs to one of the three countable groups. If a correction is needed, cross out the mistaken entry with one line, write the corrected value beside it, and add initials; do not erase or obscure the original. State that the guide should not present totals, cleanup results, or claims about what was collected, because those figures will not be known when the instructions are written.

Close with a concise end-of-shift checklist that covers matching labels to records, confirming that the final sheet is legible, returning the scales and reusable tubs to the staging area, and reporting unresolved questions to Luis or Mara. Keep the guide practical and specific to the facts above. could you make a short summary of the notes below for someone who just moved to the neighborhood? keep it to one paragraph and explain how the book exchange works, including when and where it happens. i think the bit about not having to leave a book is important, because people sometimes assume it's a strict swap. maybe mention the volunteer setup too, but don't make it sound like there's a staffed shop every day. these are the notes from our flyer and the notice on the shelf:

The Maple Street Book Exchange is at the corner of Maple and Third, in the former bus shelter beside the community garden. It is open on Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Volunteers set out the books and tidy the shelves during those hours. The exchange is free. Visitors are welcome to take a book without leaving one; bringing a book to share is encouraged, but it is not required. The shelves include fiction, children’s books, cookbooks, and local history. Please leave books in readable condition, and don’t leave magazines or textbooks. If the shelter is closed because of heavy rain, the weekly opening will be announced on the neighborhood noticeboard. The exchange is run by residents, not by the library.", "output": "Write a short, one-paragraph summary of the information below for someone who has just moved to the neighborhood. Explain how the book exchange works, including where and when it is open. Make clear that visitors may take a book without leaving one, that sharing a book is encouraged but not required, and that residents run the exchange with volunteer help rather than operating a staffed shop every day. Include the types of books available and the rules about donations. Mention what happens if heavy rain closes the shelter. The source notes also say that the exchange is free and is not run by the library.

The Maple Street Book Exchange is at the corner of Maple and Third, in the former bus shelter beside the community garden. Visitors are welcome to take a book without leaving one; bringing a book to share is encouraged, but it is not required. The shelves include fiction, children’s books, cookbooks, and local history.
